analysis.one_liner: Ended Major League Baseball's special exemption from the nation's antitrust laws.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to strip baseball's unique antitrust exemption, introduced four months after the strike that wiped out the 1994 World Series, never received a committee vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Baseball is the only major American sport whose business practices are shielded from federal antitrust law, a protection dating to a 1922 court ruling. This bill would have amended the Clayton Act to apply antitrust law to major league baseball, letting players and competitors challenge practices like the reserve system in court. It left several areas alone on purpose: the amateur draft, the minor league reserve clause, minor league agreements, restrictions on teams moving to new cities, and televised-game rules covered by a 1961 law.
analysis.who_benefits: Major league players would gain the standing to sue over restraints like the reserve clause, the same lever football and basketball players used to win free agency. Fans and taxpayers in cities that lose or nearly lose teams would gain a way to challenge monopoly behavior. Sports businesses competing with baseball for players, stadiums, and broadcasting would face a level playing field.

how_it_helps.text: Makes the antitrust laws apply to the business of professional major league baseball by adding a new section to the Clayton Act, putting baseball on the same legal footing as other professional sports.
Would let players and other parties take baseball's restraints of trade to federal court, ending the sport's status as the only major league shielded from antitrust suits.

Narrows the change deliberately: the amateur draft, the minor league reserve clause, the Professional Baseball Agreement, franchise relocation rules, and the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961 would all be unaffected, so the bill targeted the core major league exemption rather than rewriting every rule in the sport.

analysis.who_pays: Major league club owners and the league office would bear the cost: the exemption has protected player restraints, coordinated league rules, and monopoly economics from antitrust scrutiny since 1922. Exposed to suits, owners could face damages, litigation costs, and loss of control over how they contract with players.

drawbacks.text: The bill only partially ends the exemption: the amateur draft, the minor league reserve clause, the Professional Baseball Agreement, franchise relocation restrictions, and the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961 would remain outside antitrust law, so much of baseball's special legal treatment would survive even if it passed.

Opening league rules to antitrust suits invites years of litigation over player contracts and league governance, with unpredictable results for a sport just emerging from a 232-day strike that had already canceled the World Series — a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

The bill says nothing about ticket prices, broadcasting, or any direct consumer protection; its benefits to fans would come indirectly, through competition and player leverage rather than through any enforceable right.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For players and fans, the benefit is real but indirect: the bill would hand them the same legal tool other sports' players used to win free agency, and it would expose baseball's monopoly economics to challenge. The costs fall almost entirely on owners — litigation risk and loss of a century-old legal shield — which is the point of the bill. The main design weakness is the long list of carve-outs, which would have left the draft, the minor leagues, and relocation restrictions untouched; supporters chose a narrow target over a clean repeal, likely to make it harder to oppose.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Jim Bunning, a Hall of Fame pitcher turned Republican congressman, introduced the bill on May 11, 1995, joined as an original cosponsor by five colleagues — four Democrats and two Republicans — shortly after the longest strike in baseball history ended.

The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on the day of introduction, and the action record shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action at any point afterward.
It remained at that stage for the rest of the 104th Congress, which ended January 3, 1997, so it never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major league owners, who kept the antitrust exemption that shields their player and league rules from court challenges, plus the committee leadership that avoided a politically awkward vote in the aftermath of the strike.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican sponsor with 4 Democratic and 2 Republican cosponsors — but only 7 of 435 House members ever backed it, and no votes were ever taken.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped the exemption that has shielded baseball's cartel — above all the reserve system binding players to clubs — from antitrust suits since 1922. Owners' interest in keeping it runs directly against players' bargaining power and fans' exposure to monopoly pricing and team behavior.

Players are the workers the reserve system restrains; antitrust exposure would have given them the same court leverage football and basketball players used to win free agency. Because players are labor rather than an industry, their gain is the public's gain here.

The bill expressly leaves the minor league reserve clause, the Professional Baseball Agreement, and all other minor league matters outside antitrust law, so the affiliated minor leagues' controlled structure would be locked in place even under reform.
